payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make this look like a comic book photo
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image retain the photographic subject matter while presenting it as a comic-book photo?
node.criteria: Compare SOURCE and EDITED: the subject matter should remain recognizable as the supplied photograph's subject, with a photographic appearance rather than being wholly replaced by an unrelated scene or purely non-photographic depiction.
node.binding: The requested endpoint is a comic-book photo, so the comic-book treatment must still read as a photo of the supplied subject.
node.source_quote: Make this look like a comic book photo
node.endpoint: The edited image presents the supplied photographic subject matter in a comic-book photo treatment.
node.necessity: A comic-book treatment that loses the photographic subject matter would not fulfill the requested kind of image.
node.zero_when: EDITED does not retain recognizable photographic subject matter from SOURCE; unrelated changes do not count.
node.half_when: The subject remains partly recognizable or photographic, but substantial parts of the image no longer read as the supplied photo.
node.full_when: The supplied subject matter remains recognizable and the result reads as a photograph given comic-book styling.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image retains the recognizable source scene—an urban intersection with the same buildings, traffic light, cars, and pedestrian—and still looks photographic. However, it shows little clear comic-book styling, so the requested comic-book-photo treatment is only weakly achieved despite preserving the subject matter.

response.content: {"text":"The binding is too narrow: it checks preservation of photographic subject matter but does not make the requested comic-book treatment an independently necessary part of fulfillment. The trace confirms the intersection remains recognizable and photographic, yet reports little clear comic styling; that is evidence of incomplete requested progress, not a transport or dependency failure. Revise the typed criterion/binding so it separately assesses recognizable source subject matter and visible comic-book styling, and makes the endpoint require both. Keep partial credit for genuine but incomplete styling, and do not let preserved content alone satisfy the request. The reference “no” constrains the aggregate, but does not establish that no change occurred; resolve the tension with the rubric’s partial-progress rule using the images and explicit styling evidence rather than forcing the reference label."}
